title: Get Certified

learn.summary: This is the single most important node on this roadmap: no app replaces hands-on practice with a manikin and an instructor. A Red Cross or AHA First Aid/CPR/AED course takes about 4–6 hours, costs roughly the price of a nice dinner, and certifies you for two years. Everything else here is preparation for — not replacement of — that class.

do: Book an in-person First Aid/CPR/AED course this week — search redcross.org/take-a-class or cpr.heart.org for a session near you and actually register.

children.title: Finding a Course

learn.summary: Both the American Red Cross and the American Heart Association run searchable course locators; look for 'Adult First Aid/CPR/AED' as the standard all-in-one. Blended courses do the theory online and skills in person in about 2 hours — a good option for busy schedules. Employers often reimburse the fee; workplaces, gyms, and community centers frequently host classes.

do: Find three course dates within 30 minutes of you, pick one, and put it in your calendar with the registration confirmation.

children.title: What Certification Covers

learn.summary: A standard course teaches adult CPR (30 compressions to 2 breaths), AED use, choking response, bleeding control, and recognition of stroke, heart attack, and shock — with graded practice on manikins until compression depth (at least 2 inches) and rate (100–120/min) are correct. Certification lasts 2 years. Pediatric and wilderness modules are separate add-ons worth considering for parents and hikers.

do: If you were ever certified, check the date on your old card today — if it's more than 2 years old, you're due for renewal.

children.title: Hands-Only CPR Awareness

learn.summary: Until you're trained, know the untrained-bystander version the AHA promotes: if an adult collapses and isn't breathing normally, call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100–120 beats per minute — the tempo of 'Stayin' Alive' — and don't stop until help takes over. Bystander CPR can double or triple survival from cardiac arrest. This awareness is a bridge to training, not a substitute for it.

do: Practice the 100–120 bpm rhythm today by pressing on a firm cushion to 'Stayin' Alive' for 2 minutes straight — notice how tiring it is; real CPR is harder.
